claims.text: HEA nanoparticle stability at operating temperature is governed by the balance between temperature-activated atomic diffusion and local lattice strain.
Differences in constituent atomic radii produce local lattice distortion in solid-solution alloys.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch increases lattice strain.
Greater lattice strain raises the energy barriers for atomic hopping and diffusion.
Elevated diffusion barriers delay or prevent phase segregation and compositional instability.
Insufficient lattice strain produces lower diffusion barriers and enables elemental redistribution at elevated temperature.
The starting nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase HEA solid solutions with five or more metals distributed uniformly at near-equal atomic ratios.
Compositional tuning can systematically vary atomic-size mismatch and thereby modulate lattice strain.
Atomic mobility increases at elevated temperature.
Low-strain nanoparticles undergo more rapid diffusion, elemental redistribution, and phase segregation than high-strain nanoparticles.
High-strain nanoparticles will retain a single-phase structure and uniform composition throughout 473–1923 K.
High-strain nanoparticles will have lower atomic hopping rates and diffusion coefficients than low-strain counterparts.
Low-strain nanoparticles will begin ordering or phase separation at a lower critical temperature than high-strain nanoparticles.
The proposed strain-controlled stability relationship will hold under both inert and mildly reactive conditions unless surface passivation or strong metal-support interactions dominate.
The critical temperature for diffusion-driven segregation varies with lattice strain and composition.
Environmental chemistry can alter the structure and oxide-phase content of HEA nanoparticles.
In situ XRD, TEM/EDS, and molecular-dynamics simulations can jointly quantify phase segregation, elemental redistribution, lattice strain, and diffusion kinetics in the proposed comparison.
